opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think it's one where image generation is in a slightly different position than, say, language models working on math or code. In those domains you have this wonderful property where you can check the answer: the proof goes through, the unit tests pass, the number matches. That gives you a clean reward signal, and we've seen how powerful reinforcement learning becomes once you have that.

With images, most of what we care about is fundamentally subjective. Is this beautiful? Is this the mood the person wanted? There's no ground truth for that. But I think people underestimate how much of image generation actually *is* verifiable, or at least partially verifiable. If someone asks for three red apples on a blue plate, you can count the apples. You can check the colors. You can check spatial relationships: is the cat to the left of the dog? Text rendering is a great example. If the prompt says the sign should read "Open 24 Hours," you can run OCR and check whether it does. Those are exactly the areas where models have historically been weakest, and they're the areas where verification is most tractable.

So I see a kind of split. For compositional correctness, prompt adherence, counting, text, physical plausibility to some extent, we can build verifiers, often using other models like strong vision-language models or detectors, and use those as reward signals. That lets you push on the parts of the problem where "correct" is well defined, without needing a human to label every sample.

The caveat, and it's a big one, is reward hacking. Verifiers built from models have blind spots, and generative models are extremely good at finding them. You optimize hard against a counting checker and you might get images that technically have three apples but look strange, or you lose diversity and aesthetic quality. So you have to be careful to treat verifiable rewards as one component, balanced against preference signals and regularization that keeps you close to the distribution of good images.

Longer term, I'm excited about this pushing image models toward something more like reasoning: planning a layout, checking it, revising. Once you have a way to say "this part is wrong," you can let the model iterate, and that starts to look a lot like the test-time compute ideas that have worked so well in language. I don't think verifiability will solve the aesthetic side of the problem, but it can take a lot of the frustrating failures off the table, and that frees people to focus on the creative part.

r001.rationale: It proposes verifiers for counting, colors, spatial relationships, text, and plausibility, but does not propose rewarding consistency across 3D reconstructions from multiple camera views.

r002.rationale: It discusses verifier blind spots and reward hacking, but does not identify obtaining a broad range of verifiable domains as a challenge to generalizing improvements.

r003.rationale: It says image qualities such as beauty and mood are subjective and lack ground truth, contrasting them with domains where answers can be checked.

r004.rationale: It says verifiable rewards can improve well-defined aspects and reduce frustrating failures, but does not suggest those gains will improve generation outside the verifiable domains.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because so much of the recent progress in language models has come from exactly that: domains like math and code where you can check the answer. You generate a proof, you run it through a verifier. You write a program, you run the tests. That gives you a clean reward signal, and once you have that, reinforcement learning can really take off.

Images are harder because, for most of what people actually want, there's no ground truth. If I ask for "a cozy cabin at dusk," there are a million valid answers and no function that tells me which one is correct. Aesthetic quality, mood, style, those are fundamentally subjective, and that's where a lot of the value lives.

But I don't think it's all or nothing. There are pockets of image generation that are surprisingly verifiable. Text rendering is the obvious one. If I ask for a sign that says "Open," I can OCR the output and check whether it says "Open." Counting is another, how many apples, how many people. Spatial relations, is the cup to the left of the laptop. Those can be checked with a detector or a VQA model, and they're exactly the things that models have historically been bad at. Then there's the whole class of editing tasks where the constraint is consistency: change the shirt color but keep everything else the same. You can measure that pretty directly.

What's exciting to me is that these verifiable pieces tend to be the parts where users are most frustrated. Nobody complains that a model's lighting is a little off; they complain that it got the wrong number of fingers or mangled their text. So even if we can only verify a slice of the problem, that slice overlaps a lot with what people care about.

The caveat is that you have to be careful about what you're optimizing. If your verifier is a learned model, the generator will find its blind spots and exploit them. You get images that satisfy the checker but look worse to a human. So I see verifiable domains as a way to nail down the correctness floor, the things that should just work, while human preference data still has to shape the ceiling. The long-term picture is probably a mix, where the verifiable signals keep the model honest and the softer signals keep it beautiful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses text, counting, spatial relations, and editing as verifiable tasks, but does not propose using consistency across generated camera views or 3D reconstructions as a reward.

r002.rationale: It says only a slice of image generation may be verifiable, but does not identify obtaining a broad range of verifiable domains as a challenge to generalizing improvements beyond them.

r003.rationale: The response says aesthetic quality, mood, and style are subjective and lack a ground truth, unlike accuracy checks such as OCR or tests.

r004.rationale: The response says verifiable signals can establish a correctness floor, but does not suggest that improving a few verifiable domains will improve generation outside those domains.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is using verifiable tasks to give image models a more reliable learning signal. With an image, it’s often hard to specify what makes it good—there’s a lot of subjectivity. But there are aspects you can check: did it generate the right number of objects? Is the text correct? Are the spatial relationships consistent with the prompt?

If you can verify those properties reliably, you can potentially use that feedback to improve the model, rather than relying entirely on human judgments of which image looks better. The interesting question is whether learning on those narrower tasks transfers to more general image generation.

The caveat is that your verifier only captures part of what you care about. You could satisfy every measurable constraint and still produce an unappealing image. So I see this as a promising signal for improving correctness and control, alongside the signals that teach a model visual quality.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verifiable object counts, text, and spatial relationships, but does not propose checking consistency across multiple camera views or 3D reconstructions.

r002.rationale: It raises whether learning on narrower tasks transfers to general image generation, but does not identify obtaining a sufficiently broad range of verifiable domains as a challenge.

r003.rationale: It says image quality is subjective and hard to specify, while properties like object counts and text can be checked, communicating that aesthetic quality is harder to measure than accuracy.

r004.rationale: The response asks whether learning on narrower tasks transfers to general generation; it does not suggest that maximizing quality in a few verifiable domains could improve generation elsewhere.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting thing about verifiable domains is that they give you a way to check whether a generated image actually satisfies what you asked for. An image can look very convincing and still get the number of objects wrong or put them in the wrong spatial relationship. If you can verify those properties, you have a much more concrete learning signal than visual plausibility alone.

That could let you generate candidates, check them, and use that feedback to improve the model. The challenge is making sure that improvement carries beyond the things you can easily verify. But I think it’s a promising way to push image generation toward following instructions more reliably.

r001.rationale: The response discusses verifying object counts and spatial relationships, but does not propose using consistency across multiple camera views or 3D reconstructions as a reward signal.

r002.rationale: It notes the challenge of carrying improvements beyond properties that are easy to verify, but does not identify obtaining a sufficiently broad range of verifiable domains as the challenge.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare the difficulty of measuring aesthetic quality with measuring accuracy.
